text: HPAI (H5N1) should be suspected whenever a flock or village sees sudden, high mortality. Because lesions don't have time to develop with such rapid death, do NOT perform a necropsy — instead call the district vet or the NaVRI hotline directly (012 833-795 or 012 214-970), who will need the carcasses for lab analysis. Severity can range from mild with little mortality to a rapidly spreading, highly fatal epidemic; wild waterfowl (e.g. wild ducks) tend to be more resistant than domestic poultry, and a virus causing no visible disease in waterfowl can still be highly pathogenic in domestic birds. In very acute form, birds stop eating, hunch with head drawn in and ruffled feathers, and die within hours. Less acute signs: heavy/difficult breathing, head paralysis/tremor, swollen bluish comb and wattles, and hemorrhages under the leg skin. In ducks, symptoms are often milder: sleepiness with head touching the ground, white/cloudy eyes, and swollen eyelids. Transmission is mainly through feces — waterfowl act as a reservoir, carrying and shedding the virus in their gut without necessarily being sick. There is no treatment. Prevention relies entirely on biosecurity: quarantine newly purchased birds in isolation before introducing them to the flock, since incubating birds can look healthy; net enclosures to keep wild birds (potential silent carriers) away from housed poultry; and washing shoes/hands with soap after visiting a live bird market to avoid carrying the virus home.
